# Reflection & Learnings {#sec-reflection}

## Challenges & Lessons Learned

**Building on data we invented ourselves.** We had no access to real customer data. The tariffs are real — 65 documents of published provider pricing — but the customers are invented: six personas, their subscriptions, and roughly two thousand synthetic trip legs. This was more work than it sounds — the travel histories had to be irregular enough to be worth analysing, since a perfectly regular commuter makes every recommendation trivial. But it also means we were marking our own homework. The engine prices real tariffs correctly against behaviour we designed, and we have no way of knowing how it behaves against a real customer who takes an unexplained Uber every third Friday. The provider connection step in the onboarding is simulated for the same reason. We designed the interaction as though it were real, which we think is the right way round: the pattern is testable now, and only the data source would need replacing.

**How we worked.** We met every Wednesday around the lecture, went through what had been finished over the previous weekend, and agreed on what came next. The actual implementation then happened individually or in pairs, mostly on weekends. For five people with different timetables this worked better than trying to coordinate continuously, but it had one obvious cost: something broken on a Saturday usually stayed broken until Wednesday. What made it hold together was structure we set up early — a GitHub repository with clear ownership per area and a Notion workspace for planning — so that our work rarely collided in terms of responsibility, even when it occasionally collided in the same file.

**The last few weeks.** The last stretch of the project overlapped with exam period for all five of us. It was a stressful few weeks, but not a damaging one — the substantial work was already done, and what remained was integration and writing. The rule is simple: finish the work that needs concentration before the calendar gets crowded, because the work that survives a crowded calendar is the small stuff.

## Limitations & Next Steps

**The data.** The tariff data is real but it is a snapshot: price changes would need a refresh mechanism the prototype does not have. The customers are synthetic, so our evaluation shows the engine prices real tariffs correctly against behaviour we invented, not how the recommendations hold up against a real person's messier travel. The provider connection in the onboarding is simulated rather than integrated.

**The model.** Where the system compares a mode the customer did not actually use, CO~2~ and duration come from hand-authored per-mode averages rather than route data; the code notes explicitly that the speed figures have no empirical source behind them. A structural property of the domain also limits the multi-criteria scoring: within a single category the alternatives do not change how the person travels, so emissions and time are identical across them and cost decides. The CO~2~ and flexibility weights only become decisive in the cross-category comparison. The forecaster, for its part, depends on calendar entries being present and readable, and falls back to its deterministic baseline when they are not.

**The scope.** The system reasons about one person at a time, so shared household or employer-funded arrangements cannot be modelled at all.

**Next steps.** Three things would matter most. Replacing the simulated provider connection with a real OAuth import — starting with the Deutschlandticket, whose flat tariff keeps the integration simple — would let us test the recommendations against travel someone actually took rather than travel we invented. Adding route-level emissions and duration data from a routing service would give the CO~2~ and time axes enough resolution to actually change a recommendation, which the hand-authored averages cannot. And extending the evaluation from a single analysis run to rolling time windows would test the claim the product is built on, namely that the advice stays correct as someone's behaviour changes. None of these require redesigning anything: the tariff knowledge base is file-driven, and the scoring engine takes its weights as parameters rather than hard-coding them.
